newsitem.title: USA: Texas hospital pays $9.5 mln in drugged doctor case.
newsitem.headline: Texas hospital pays $9.5 mln in drugged doctor case.

text.p: A Texas hospital agreed on Wednesday to pay $9.5 million in damages to the family of a woman and her unborn child who died two years ago while in the care of a drug-impaired doctor.

South Park Hospital and Medical Center in Lubbock, Texas, also agreed to push for random screening of its doctors for drug abuse, and for a state legislative review of laws that keep secret any evidence of wrongdoing by doctors.
"We are elated," said Richard Mithoff, the attorney for plaintiff Jake Glickman, whose daughter died while in labor with her first child at the hospital on July 4, 1995.
"This is the most far-reaching medical malpractice judgment I am aware of -- not just financially for the family but more importantly because it requires the hospital to clean house," Mithoff said.
Margo Glickman Johnson, then aged 20, was admitted into South Park Hospital to give birth to her son and was given an epidural anesthetic by Dr. Jack Dunn during labor.
But Dunn, who had allegedly been using drugs for a long time, missed the epidural space in her lower back, instead puncturing the vena cava, a large vein that leads directly to the heart.
Glickman Johnson suffered a cardiac arrest and died shortly afterwards. Hospital staff allegedly made no effort to deliver the unborn child, who died with his mother.
The hospital had been aware of Dunn's alleged drug use for five months before Glickman Johnson's death, but had allowed him to continue working while checking his background.

Under the out-of-court agreement approved by State District Judge John Forbis on Wednesday, Jake Glickman was awarded $5 million, the dead woman's husband David Johnson was awarded $3.5 million and her mother Mercy McGee received $1 million.
The three plaintiffs will also split a separate $1 million cash settlement agreed with Dr. Dunn last year.
South Park Hospital denied liability but decided not to contest the lawsuit.

"We hope the agreement provides the family with some peace of mind...and we will continue to review our medical staff credentialing process," Clint Matthews, chief executive officer at South Park Hospital, told Reuters.

The hospital apologized to Glickman Johnson's family in the formal agreement. "South Park shares Glickman's desires to adopt changes to its policies, practices and procedures in order to prevent future recurrences of this tragic event."
South Park was owned by OrNda HealthCorp of Nashville, Tenn. at the time of the incident but is now owned by Tenet Healthcare Corporation of Santa Barbara, Calif.
